SECTION 010:00–6:26

Allow row exchanges: PA = LU

The permutation matrix records the ordering needed for elimination.

Lecture 4 obtained A = LU when elimination needed no row exchanges. Lecture 5 completes the picture: even an invertible matrix can have zero in a pivot position, requiring a different row to be brought into that position.

A permutation matrix P records the row reordering. The factorization becomes

PA = LU.

Here L is lower triangular with ones on the diagonal, while U is upper triangular with the pivots on its diagonal. Left multiplication by P rearranges A’s rows. If the original row order already works, P = I and the formula reduces to A = LU.

Strang states this factorization for every invertible square A. The permutation puts the rows in an order that allows elimination to finish with nonzero pivots.

Algebra and numerical accuracy. The lecture distinguishes exchanges needed to avoid a zero pivot from exchanges used to avoid very small pivots in computer arithmetic. This edition follows its algebraic discussion. The MATLAB remarks are retained as part of the historical lecture.

SECTION 026:26–10:15

Count and undo row reorderings

P is the identity with its rows rearranged, and P⁻¹ = Pᵀ.

Start with the n × n identity matrix and rearrange its rows. The result has one 1 in each row and each column and zeros elsewhere. Applied on the left, it performs the same rearrangement on any matrix with n rows.

There are n choices for the first row, n − 1 for the second, and so on. Therefore

Number of n × n permutation matrices = n! = n(n − 1) ··· 2 · 1.

This gives 24 permutations for four rows and 120 for five rows. Keeping the rows in their original order counts too: it gives the identity permutation.

Every reordering can be undone. The inverse permutation matrix is its transpose:

P⁻¹ = Pᵀ,   PᵀP = PPᵀ = I.

The reason is visible in the dot products of its columns. Each column is a different standard basis vector; it has dot product 1 with itself and 0 with every other column. Thus PᵀP is I. Strang points out that other matrices also have transpose equal to inverse; permutations are one special family.

SECTION 0310:15–12:46

Transpose a rectangular matrix

Rows become columns, and the dimensions switch.

For the first transpose example, call the displayed three-by-two matrix B. Its columns become the rows of Bᵀ:

B=[132341],BT=[124331]

B has three rows and two columns. Bᵀ has two rows and three columns. In general, transposition sends an m × n matrix to an n × m matrix.

(Bᵀ)ᵢⱼ = Bⱼᵢ.

The entry in row i, column j of the transpose comes from row j, column i of the original. Transposing twice restores every entry to its original position: (Bᵀ)ᵀ = B.

SECTION 0412:46–15:06

Recognize a symmetric matrix

A square matrix is symmetric when transposing leaves it unchanged.

A symmetric matrix satisfies Sᵀ = S. Since transposition switches the matrix dimensions, this equality requires S to be square.

The lecture’s example is

S=[317129794]

The 1 above the diagonal matches the 1 below it. So do the two 7s and the two 9s. The diagonal entries stay where they are under transposition.

Sᵢⱼ = Sⱼᵢ for every pair of indices.

Symmetry concerns these matching entries. It does not require positive entries, even though Strang happens to choose positive numbers here. Nor is it the same property as a transpose giving the inverse: Sᵀ = S and Pᵀ = P⁻¹ are different conditions.

SECTION 0515:06–17:16

Multiply RᵀR to create symmetry

Paired dot products produce equal entries across the diagonal.

Take the two-by-three matrix R = Bᵀ. The product RᵀR has dimensions (3 × 2)(2 × 3), so its result is three-by-three:

[132341][124331]=[1011711131171117]

Its (1, 1) entry is 1² + 3² = 10. The (1, 2) entry is 1·2 + 3·3 = 11, while the (2, 1) entry is 2·1 + 3·3 = 11. Reversing those two column vectors does not change their dot product.

Likewise, the (1, 3) and (3, 1) entries are both 7. Completing the remaining products gives 13 at (2, 2), 11 at both (2, 3) and (3, 2), and 17 at (3, 3).

More generally, entry (i, j) of RᵀR is column i of R dotted with column j of R. Swapping i and j gives the same scalar. That explains the symmetry entry by entry.

SECTION 0617:16–20:17

Prove the symmetry without numbers

Reverse the product order when taking its transpose.

The numerical example suggests a general fact. For any real rectangular matrix R, the square matrix RᵀR is symmetric.

Use the transpose rule for a product and remember that it reverses the factors:

(AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ.

Apply that rule with A = Rᵀ and B = R:

(RᵀR)ᵀ = Rᵀ(Rᵀ)ᵀ = RᵀR.

Transposing the product returns the original product, which is precisely the condition for symmetry. The key second step is that a double transpose gives back R.

No special values from the example are needed. If R has m rows and n columns, RᵀR is always an n × n symmetric matrix. This argument establishes symmetry; it makes no claim here that the product is invertible.

SECTION 0720:17–26:43

A vector space allows linear combinations

Start with R²: all real two-component vectors.

The lecture now shifts from individual matrix operations to whole spaces of vectors. Its two basic operations are vector addition and multiplication by a scalar. Combining them gives linear combinations, such as cv + dw.

The first example is R², the set of all column vectors with two real entries. Strang lists (3, 2)ᵀ, (0, 0)ᵀ, and (π, e)ᵀ. Addition and scalar multiplication operate on their components.

(3, 2)ᵀ + (π, e)ᵀ = (3 + π, 2 + e)ᵀ.

Every such result is still in R². Geometrically, R² is the entire coordinate plane: a vector’s first component gives its horizontal coordinate, and its second gives its vertical coordinate.

The origin cannot be removed

Multiplying any vector by zero gives the zero vector. Adding a vector to its opposite also gives zero. If the plane were punctured by removing the origin, these operations would leave the set.

0(3, 2)ᵀ = (0, 0)ᵀ,
(3, 2)ᵀ + (−3, −2)ᵀ = (0, 0)ᵀ.

Every vector space contains its zero vector. More generally, vector-space operations must satisfy the usual algebraic axioms. In Rⁿ those rules already hold; when considering a subset with the inherited operations, the central question is whether the results stay inside it.

SECTION 0826:43–29:51

Count components to identify Rⁿ

A zero component still counts as a component.

R³ contains all vectors with three real components. In particular, (3, 2, 0)ᵀ belongs to R³. The last component being zero does not turn it into a two-component vector.

In general,

Rⁿ = { (x₁, x₂, …, xₙ)ᵀ : every xᵢ is real }.

The lecture uses column vectors throughout this discussion. Addition combines corresponding entries; multiplying by a real scalar multiplies every entry. Both operations keep the number of components fixed.

The ambient space tells us what kind of vectors we are using. A line inside R² contains two-component vectors even though only one parameter is needed to move along it. Similarly, a plane inside R³ contains three-component vectors.

Keep two questions separate

How many components does each vector have? How many independent directions does the space contain? A one-dimensional line can sit inside R², R³, or a higher-dimensional space.

Strang notes that vector addition and scalar multiplication must obey the usual algebraic rules. For these real coordinate vectors they do. The next examples ask whether restricting the set preserves the required operations.

SECTION 0929:51–31:31

Why one quadrant is not a vector space

Closure under addition alone is not enough.

Take only vectors whose two components are nonnegative:

Q = { (x, y)ᵀ : x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0 }.

Adding two vectors in Q stays in Q. For example, (3, 2)ᵀ + (5, 6)ᵀ = (8, 8)ᵀ. Each new component is still nonnegative.

Multiplication by every real scalar fails. As Strang points out, multiplying (3, 2)ᵀ by −5 sends it to the opposite quadrant:

−5(3, 2)ᵀ = (−15, −10)ᵀ ∉ Q.

The term closed means that performing an operation on elements of the set produces another element of that set. Q is closed under addition, but is not closed under multiplication by all real scalars. It is therefore not a real vector space with the usual operations.

Notice that Q does contain zero. Having zero is necessary for a subspace, but by itself it does not guarantee that the other closure requirements hold.

SECTION 1031:31–35:48

A subspace must keep every linear combination

A whole line through the origin works; a shifted line fails.

A subspace is itself a vector space inside another vector space, using the same addition and scalar multiplication. For a nonempty subset of Rⁿ, this can be tested by checking that sums and all real scalar multiples remain inside it.

Suppose a subspace contains a nonzero vector v. It must then contain every multiple tv, including negative multiples and the zero multiple. Those multiples fill an entire line through the origin.

L = { tv : t ∈ R }.

This line also passes the addition test: sv + tv = (s + t)v stays on the line. Multiplying tv by another scalar c gives (ct)v, again on the line. So all multiples of v form a subspace.

A line that does not pass through the origin fails immediately. Multiplying any of its vectors by zero reaches the origin, which is missing from that shifted line.

The subspace test

For a nonempty subset S of Rⁿ, require cv + dw ∈ S whenever v, w ∈ S and c, d are real. This combines addition and scalar multiplication in one condition.

SECTION 1135:48–39:47

List the possible subspaces in R² and R³

Include the zero subspace and the entire ambient space.

The lecture lists every kind of subspace of R²:

  • The zero subspace {0}, containing only (0, 0)ᵀ.
  • Any whole line through the origin.
  • All of R².

The zero subspace is valid: 0 + 0 = 0, and every scalar times 0 is 0. The whole space is always a subspace of itself.

A line inside R² resembles R¹, but its vectors still have two components. It is a one-dimensional subspace of R², rather than literally the set of one-component vectors R¹.

Why are there no other possibilities in R²? If a subspace contains a nonzero vector, it contains the whole line through it. If it also contains a vector off that line, combinations of the two directions fill the entire plane.

In R³ the corresponding list is {0}, any line through the origin, any plane through the origin, or all of R³. A shifted plane, like a shifted line, fails because it does not contain zero.

Expanded explanation. The two-direction argument explains why the lecture’s R² list is complete. The figures show schematic representatives of each type, rather than specific extra board examples.

SECTION 1239:47–43:42

Create a subspace from a matrix’s columns

Include all their linear combinations, not only the columns themselves.

Strang returns to the three-by-two matrix and calls it A:

A=[132341]

Its columns a₁ = (1, 2, 4)ᵀ and a₂ = (3, 3, 1)ᵀ are vectors in R³. A set containing only those two vectors is not a subspace. It also needs their sum, their multiples, zero, and every combination obtained by those operations.

[124]+[331]=[455]

Include all real linear combinations of the columns to obtain the column space:

C(A) = { ca₁ + da₂ : c, d ∈ R }.

This really is a subspace. For example, adding ca₁ + da₂ to ea₁ + fa₂ gives (c + e)a₁ + (d + f)a₂, another combination. Multiplying by t gives (tc)a₁ + (td)a₂, another combination too. Setting both coefficients to zero includes the zero vector.

The central construction

Take the columns of a matrix and all their linear combinations. That set is its column space.

Closure written out. The algebra above expands the lecture’s statement that including all combinations guarantees a subspace.

SECTION 1343:42–47:32

See the column space as a plane

The number of components and the number of spanning directions differ.

Each nonzero column generates a line of multiples. Adding vectors from those two lines fills a plane because the two columns are not parallel. The plane passes through the origin and is the column space C(A).

For these particular columns, a multiple of (1, 2, 4)ᵀ cannot equal (3, 3, 1)ᵀ: the first coordinates would require a factor 3, while the second would then be 6 instead of 3. So the column space is larger than a line.

It remains a set of three-component vectors. It is a two-dimensional plane inside R³; it is not all of R³ and is not literally R².

Algebraic check of the drawing. Every combination has coordinates x = c + 3d, y = 2c + 3d, z = 4c + d. Substitution gives −10x + 11y − 3z = 0. This equation describes the same plane and is an editorial verification of the lecture’s geometric claim.

The same idea works beyond three dimensions

Five vectors in R¹⁰ still have ten components apiece. Their linear combinations form a subspace of R¹⁰. There may be five independent directions, or fewer: if all five vectors lie on one line, their combinations stay on that line.

The number of supplied vectors alone does not determine the dimension. Their directions and dependencies matter. Strang closes by pointing toward the next lecture: understand Ax = b using column spaces, and discover other subspaces associated with a matrix.
